mantras.anvaya_en: Subject and verb: a speaker label.

comm.t: Speaker label: the merchant now answers the king’s questions of 1.17–18 (who he is, and why he has come). Mārkaṇḍeya is still the narrator of the whole exchange.

-aḥ before a- → -o’; the m of अहम् is simply written together with the following vowel; उत्पन्नः before the voiced dh becomes उत्पन्नो (हशि च, 6.1.114).

morph.note: kta of उत् + √पद् ‘to arise’: the root’s final d and the t of the suffix become -न्न- (पद् + त → पन्न). With an intransitive verb the participle is active: ‘born, arisen’.
Genitive plural of the -in stem धनिन् ‘having wealth’ (धन + possessive -in), like बलिन् in 1.8.

mantras.anvaya: अहं समाधिः नाम वैश्यः धनिनां कुले उत्पन्नः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Name and class (समाधिः नाम वैश्यः), subject (अहम्), and a participle phrase giving his birth.
mantras.lit: I am a merchant named Samādhi, born in a family of wealthy men.
mantras.tr: I am a merchant named Samādhi, born into a wealthy family.

comm.t: The merchant answers the first question (‘who are you?’): his name, his class, his family. The next verses answer the second (‘why have you come?’).
The name समाधि — ‘composure, absorption’ — is often noticed as apt: he is the one who at the end asks the Goddess for knowledge rather than wealth (13.18), and receives it (13.25).

Final t becomes d before a vowel.
After ai the visarga stands as r before the voiced d and before the vowel ā; before the unvoiced p (दारैः पुत्रैः) it remains a visarga.

morph.note: Participle of वि + √हा ‘to leave’: ‘left without, deprived of’, construed with the instrumental (धनैः दारैः पुत्रैः).

Absolutive of आ + √दा ‘to take’. Its logical subject is not the speaker but those who wronged him — the sons and wife (or the kinsmen of 1.23): ‘having taken my wealth, (they cast me out)’. Such a shift of subject is common in epic narrative.
दार ‘wife’ is masculine and used in the plural for a single wife — a fixed idiom.

mantras.anvaya: धनलोभात् असाधुभिः पुत्रदारैः (अहं) निरस्तः च, धनैः दारैः पुत्रैः च विहीनः; (ते) मे धनम् आदाय (1.23: आप्तबन्धुभिः च निरस्तः) …
mantras.anvaya_en: Two predicates of an implied अहम् (निरस्तः, विहीनः); the absolutive phrase आदाय मे धनम् belongs with the agents who cast him out and runs into 1.23.
mantras.lit: And I have been cast out by my wicked sons and wife out of greed for wealth, and am deprived of wealth, wife and sons; (they,) having taken my wealth —
mantras.tr: My wicked sons and wife, greedy for my wealth, have driven me out. I am left without money, wife or sons; they have taken all I had,
mantras.tr_note: ‘All I had’ renders मे धनम् ‘my wealth’; the subject ‘they’ of आदाय is supplied.

comm.t: The merchant’s answer to ‘why have you come?’: his own family has thrown him out to take his wealth. His loss mirrors the king’s — Suratha was betrayed by ministers, Samādhi by sons and wife.
Unlike the king, the merchant names his betrayers as his nearest kin; the point is made sharper in 1.31–34, where he confesses that his heart still goes out to them.

flags.uncertain: The construction of the second line admits two readings: (a) धनैः दारैः पुत्रैः all depend on विहीनः (‘deprived of wealth, wife and sons’), with आदाय मे धनम् referring to the relatives; (b) विहीनः धनैः only, with दारैः पुत्रैः as the agents of आदाय (‘deprived of wealth, my wife and sons having taken it’). Reading (a) is followed here as the more natural word order.

samasa.sense: by the kinsmen he relied on

samasa.vigraha: कुशलं च अकुशलं च कुशलाकुशले (dvandva; अकुशल is a nañ tatpuruṣa); कुशलाकुशले आत्मा (स्वरूपम्) यस्याः सा, ताम्
samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (with the suffix -क) containing a dvandva
samasa.literal: whose nature is well-being and ill-being

morph.note: Present first singular of √विद् (adādi), with guṇa (विद् → वेद्) before the strong ending -मि. न वेद्मि governs प्रवृत्तिम् in 1.24.
Active kta of a verb of motion with two prefixes, अभि + आ: ‘(I) have come’ (to the forest).
आत्मक ‘having the nature of, consisting of’ (आत्मन् + -क) makes its feminine in -इका: आत्मिका. It agrees with प्रवृत्तिम् (f.) in the next verse.

mantras.anvaya: (अहं) दुःखी आप्तबन्धुभिः च निरस्तः वनम् अभ्यागतः। सः अहम् अत्र संस्थितः पुत्राणां … कुशलाकुशलात्मिकां (प्रवृत्तिं) न वेद्मि (1.24)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line ends the account of his expulsion; the second begins a sentence completed in 1.24 (न वेद्मि … प्रवृत्तिम्).
mantras.lit: — and cast out by trusted kinsmen, I have come, sorrowful, to the forest. I, such as I am, do not know the (news), of good or ill, of my sons,
mantras.tr: and, cast off by the kinsmen I trusted, I have come to this forest in grief. Now I do not know whether things go well or ill with my sons,

comm.t: The merchant’s second answer: he came to the forest because his own people drove him out. Yet his first thought is not of his wrong but of their welfare, which he cannot learn.
A modern reading: he has been thrown out and robbed, and still worries whether those who did it are well. The text shows the bond outliving the betrayal before it names it as a puzzle (1.31–34).

sandhi.joined: किं नु तेषां गृहे क्षेममक्षेमं किं
sandhi.split: किम् + नु + तेषाम् + गृहे + क्षेमम् + अक्षेमम् + किम्
sandhi.note: Final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra (किं, तेषां, अक्षेमं); before the vowel of अक्षेमम् the m of क्षेमम् stays m and is written with it.

samasa.alt: Also read as ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, स्वस्य जनाः ‘one’s own people’; the sense is the same.

morph.note: kta of सम् + √स्था (स्था → स्थि before -त), active: ‘(I,) remaining (here)’. It gives the reason he has no news.
किम् … किम् as particles: ‘is it … or is it …?’, a double question. The particle नु adds anxious wondering.

mantras.anvaya: अत्र संस्थितः (अहं) पुत्राणां स्वजनानां च दाराणां च प्रवृत्तिं न वेद्मि (1.23)। तेषां गृहे साम्प्रतं क्षेमं किं नु, अक्षेमं किं नु?
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes न वेद्मि of 1.23 with its object; the second is a double question (किं नु … किं नु).
mantras.lit: — (the news) of my own people and of my wife, staying here. Is it, I wonder, welfare in their house, or ill-fare, at present?
mantras.tr: or with my kin and my wife, for I am here, far away. Is all well in their home now, or is it not?
mantras.tr_note: ‘Far away’ draws out अत्र संस्थितः (‘staying here’), which explains why he has no news.

comm.t: The sentence of 1.23 ends: he has no tidings of sons, kin or wife because he is here in the forest. He asks twice, with किं नु, whether they are well.

The t of सत् becomes d before the voiced v. (The digital source marked the half-form d with a joiner, removed as an encoding hint; the letters are unchanged.)
Before the unvoiced k the visarga remains. Inside दुर्वृत्त, the prefix दुस् shows r before the voiced v (ससजुषो रुः, 8.2.66).

morph.note: कथम् ‘how?’ asks after their condition in general (‘how are they?’); the following किं नु … किं नु asks the narrower question of their conduct.

mantras.anvaya: ते कथम्? मे सुताः सद्वृत्ताः किं नु, दुर्वृत्ताः किं नु?
mantras.anvaya_en: A short question (कथं ते) and a double question with किं नु … किं नु.
mantras.lit: How are they? Are my sons, I wonder, of good conduct, or of bad conduct?
mantras.tr: How are they? Are my sons living rightly now, or have they gone astray?

comm.t: The merchant ends his answer with anxious questions about the very sons who robbed him. The king will ask next (1.27–28) why he still cares for them.
A modern reading: he does not ask whether they regret what they did, only whether they are good. Attachment here takes the form of hope for those who caused the hurt.
